'''Lee Bontecou''' (January 15, 1931 – November 8, 2022) was an American sculptor and printmaker and a pioneer figure in the New York art world. She kept her work consistently in a recognizable style, and received broad recognition in the 1960s. Bontecou made abstract sculptures in the 1960s and 1970s and created vacuum-formed plastic fish, plants, and flower forms in the 1970s. Rich, organic shapes and powerful energy appear in her drawings, prints, and sculptures. Her work has been shown and collected in many major museums in the United States and in Europe.

==Early life and education==
Bontecou was born in [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]], [[Rhode Island]].<ref name=":0" /> She had an older brother, Hank. Her father was a salesman and was involved with the development of the aluminum canoe. Her mother wired submarine parts during WWII. <ref name=":0" /> As a little girl, Bontecou spent time at the family's cabin in [[Nova Scotia|Yarmouth, Nova Scotia]], where she first experimenting with sculpture, whittling animals out of wood.<ref name=":0" /> From the time Bontecou attended high school, she found herself focusing on sculpture; "I avoided everything that was commercial art. I avoided having to make posters, and I avoided all of these... it was just not interesting to me. But I was always drawing at home, and making little clay stuff and little figures, little – anything that I could get my hands on. And I did enjoy the clay."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dore |first1=Ashton |title=Oral history interview with Lee Bontecou, 2009 January 10 |url=https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-lee-bontecou-15647#transcript |website=Archives of American Art |access-date=November 10, 2021}}</ref>

Bontecou attended Bradford Junior College (now [[Bradford College (United States)|Bradford College]]) in [[Haverhill, Massachusetts]] for her general education and then attended the [[Art Students League of New York]] from 1952 to 1955, where she studied with the sculptor [[William Zorach]].<ref name="Whitney">[http://whitney.org/Education/ForTeachers/Collection/LeeBontecou "Lee Bontecou"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141229151538/http://whitney.org/Education/ForTeachers/Collection/LeeBontecou |date=December 29, 2014 }}, [[The Whitney Museum of American Art]], Retrieved December 22, 2014.</ref> She also spent the summer of 1954 at the [[Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture]] in Maine, where she learned to weld. She received a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright scholarship]] from the [[U.S.-Italy Fulbright Commission]] to study in Rome in 1957-1958.<ref name=Whitney/> In 1971, she began teaching at [[Brooklyn College]].

Bontecou's work was deeply affected by [[WWII]]. Many of her sculptures were emotional responses to war.  Describing her own work, Bontecou said ..." I was angry...all of those- all the ones with the teeth- it was a thing of what that war was."<ref>{{cite web |title=Oral history interview with Lee Bontecou, 2009 January 10 |url=https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-lee-bontecou-15647#transcript |website=www.aaa.si.edu |language=en}}</ref>  Both her parents joined the war effort. Her mother wired transmitters for submarine navigation and her father sold gliders for the military. Later her husband, Bill Giles, would be a medic in the [[Korean War]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Oral history interview with Lee Bontecou, 2009 January 10 |url=https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-lee-bontecou-15647#transcript |website=www.aaa.si.edu |language=en}}</ref> 

==Career==
Bontecou was best known for the sculptures she created in 1959 and the 1960s, which challenged artistic conventions of both materials and presentation by hanging on the wall. They consist of welded steel frames covered with recycled canvas and industrial materials (such as conveyor belts or mail sacks) and other found objects. Her best constructions are at once mechanistic and organic, abstract but evocative of the brutality of war. Art critic [[Arthur Danto]] described them as "fierce", reminiscent of 17th-century scientist [[Robert Hooke|Robert Hooke's]] ''Micrographia'', lying "at the intersection of magnified insects, battle masks, and armored chariots...”.<ref name="Danto">Danto 2004</ref> She was one of the first female artists<ref name=":0" /> to be exhibited at [[Leo Castelli|Leo Castelli's]] art gallery in the 1960s, alongside [[Jasper Johns]], [[Frank Stella]], and [[Robert Rauschenberg]].<ref>[http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/73245/Lee-Bontecou "Lee Bontecou"], Britannica, Retrieved December 22, 2014.</ref> One of the largest examples of her work is located in the lobby of the [[David H. Koch Theater]] at [[Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts]] in [[New York City]], which was commissioned by the architect [[Philip Johnson]].<ref name="Trachtman">Trachtman, Paul. [http://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/lee-bontecous-brave-new-world-180940689/?no-ist=&page=4 "Lee Bontecou's Brave New World"], Smithsonian Magazine, Retrieved December 24, 2014.</ref> From the 1970s until 1991 she taught in the Art Department at [[Brooklyn College]].<ref name=Trachtman/>

She continued to teach through the 1990s, while spending time in Pennsylvania. She moved to [[Orbisonia, Pennsylvania]] full-time in 1988 where she continued to work.<ref name="Danto" /><ref name="Rooney 2010">{{cite journal|last=Rooney|first=Kara L.|title=Lee Bontecou: All Freedom in Every Sense|journal=The Brooklyn Rail|date=July–August 2010}}</ref> There she maintained a vigorous studio practice, but showed infrequently. She was brought back to public attention by a 2003 retrospective co-organized by the [[Hammer Museum]] in Los Angeles and the [[Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago]], that traveled to the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in New York City in 2004. The retrospective included both work from her public, art-world career and an extensive display of work done after retreating from the public view.<ref name="Danto" /> Bontecou's work was also included in the [[Carnegie International|Carnegie International 2004-5]] exhibit in [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania. In 2010, the [[Museum of Modern Art]] presented a retrospective of Bontecou's work entitled ''All Freedom in Every Sense.''<ref name="Rooney 2010"/> In 2014, her drawings were exhibited in ''Lee Bontecou: Drawn Worlds'',<ref name="archive.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.leebontecou.com/|title=Welcome to LeeBontecou.com :: Home :: Lee Bontecou, American artist whose work ranged from dark, dramatic abstract constructions to softer, transparent natural forms, evoking a correspondingly broad range of response.|date=June 29, 2007|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629100944/http://www.leebontecou.com/|archive-date=June 29, 2007}}</ref> organized by [[Menil Collection|The Menil Collection]], which traveled to the [[Princeton University Art Museum]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/lee-bontecou-menil-collection-houston|title=The Menil Collection Showcases Fifty Years of Lee Bontecou's Surreal Drawings {{!}} Architectural Digest|last=Bates|first=Rebecca|website=Architectural Digest|date=January 31, 2014|access-date=March 18, 2016}}</ref> Her work was also included in ''Revolution in the Making: Abstract Sculpture by Women, 1947-2016'' at Hauser Wirth & Schimmel in 2016.

In 2017, a major exhibition of Bontecou's drawings and sculpture, including a site-specific installation entitled ''Sandbox,'' a collaboration between Bontecou and Joan Banach, was organized by the [[Gemeentemuseum Den Haag]]. The exhibition was curated by Joan Banach and Laura Stamps, and accompanied by a fully illustrated catalogue published by Hannibal (Dutch) and Koenig Books, London (English). The catalogue contains new essays on Lee Bontecou by Laura Stamps, Curator of Modern Art at The Gemeentemuseum, Joan Banach, and Jeremy Melius, with an introduction by Gemeentemuseum Director, Benno Tempel.

==Perspective==
In the 1960s, Bontecou's work was hailed for its unique position in between painting and sculpture. Sculptor [[Donald Judd]] wrote that her work "asserts its own existence, form and power. It becomes an object in its own right."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Judd|first=Donald|date=1965|title=Lee Bontecou|journal=Arts Magazine|oclc=1580772}}</ref> The openness, autonomy, and engineering processes central to her work, were embraced by the [[Feminist art movement in the United States|Feminist Art Movement]] in the 1970s and her use of cavities and holes has been read as female genitalia, and the related, central core imagery. It is an association the artist denied.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.chicagoreader.com/chicago/lee-bontecou-doesnt-care-what-you-think/Content?oid=914734|title=Lee Bontecou Doesn't Care What You Think|last=Tapp|first=Mara|website=Chicago Reader|date=March 4, 2004|access-date=March 18, 2016}}</ref> Her work has been characterized by references to the synergy between nature and fiction, resulting naturalistically rendered creatures, with grotesquely morphed features.<ref>Butler, C., et al. Eds. 2010. Modern Women: Women Artists at the Museum of Modern Art. MoMA.</ref>

==Techniques and materials==
Bontecou worked with many materials, such as metal, paper, plastic, and fibreglass. She also worked with unconventional materials and discovered new techniques. In her drawings, she developed a process in the late 1950s of using an [[oxyacetylene torch]] to produce a carbon spray from the flame, resulting in an "airbrushed" look and deep saturated blacks that she took to her sculptural work.<ref>{{Cite news|title = 'Lee Bontecou: Drawn Worlds,' an Artist's Other Side|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/25/arts/design/lee-bontecou-drawn-worlds-an-artists-other-side.html|newspaper = The New York Times|date = July 24, 2014|access-date = December 10, 2015|issn = 0362-4331|first = Karen|last = Rosenberg}}</ref><ref name="Bontecou">{{Cite book |last1=Bontecou |first1=Lee |title=Lee Bontecou: drawn worlds |last2=White |first2=Michelle |last3=Ashton |first3=Dore |last4=Banach |first4=Joan |last5=Menil Collection (Houston |first5=Tex.) |last6=Princeton University |last7=Art Museum |date=January 1, 2014 |publisher=Menil Collection |isbn=9780300204131 |language=en |oclc=861671716}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Bontecou was married to the artist William Giles with whom she had a daughter, Valerie.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Tapp|first1=Mara|title=Lee Bontecou Doesn't Care What You Think|url=http://www.chicagoreader.com/chicago/lee-bontecou-doesnt-care-what-you-think/Content?oid=914734|website=Chicago Reader|date=March 4, 2004|access-date=February 4, 2016}}</ref>

Bontecou died in Florida on November 8, 2022, at the age of 91.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last1=Szalai |first1=Jennifer |title=Lee Bontecou, Acclaimed Creator of Wall-Mounted Art, Dies at 91 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/08/arts/lee-bontecou-dead.html |access-date=November 9, 2022 |work=New York Times |date=November 8, 2022}}</ref>

==Legacy and recognition==
In 1959, Bontecou received the [[The Louis Comfort Tiffany Foundation|Louis Comfort Tiffany Award]]. In 2004, she was elected into the [[National Academy of Design]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalacademy.org/academy/national-academicians/|title=National Academicians - National Academy Museum<!-- Bot generated title -->|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314023614/http://www.nationalacademy.org/academy/national-academicians/|archive-date=March 14, 2016}}</ref>

A picture of Bontecou working in her studio, taken by Italian photographer [[Ugo Mulas]] in 1963, was used as the cover art for [[Spoon (band)|Spoon’s]] 2007 album ''[[Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga]]''.<ref>[http://www.juxtapoz.com/music/spoon-frontman-britt-daniel-on-a-career-of-album-covers "Spoon Frontman Britt Daniel on a Career of Album Covers"], ''Juxtapoz Magazine'', Retrieved December 24, 2014.</ref> The apparently completed sculpture on the right in the aforementioned photograph is now in the collection of the [[Honolulu Museum of Art]].

Bontecou's image is included in the iconic 1972 poster [[Some Living American Women Artists (collage)|Some Living American Women Artists]] by [[Mary Beth Edelson]].<ref name="SAAM">{{cite web |title=Some Living American Women Artists/Last Supper |url=https://americanart.si.edu/artwork/some-living-american-women-artistslast-supper-76377 |website=Smithsonian American Art Museum |access-date=January 21, 2022}}</ref>
